title: Taking the train — and a preposition that changes its sound
goal: Buy a ticket, read a timetable and say how you're traveling — while learning the instrumental (*orodnik*), the last case you need at A1, along with a preposition that changes shape depending on the sound after it.
bekal: naming means of transport: *z vlakom*, *z avtobusom*, *s kolesom*, *peš*
choosing *z* or *s* from the sound of the next word
buying a ticket and asking how long the journey takes

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Na blagajni železniške postaje
dialogs.intro: The ticket counter at Ljubljana railway station, Saturday morning. Budi is heading to Bled and gets a phonetics lesson as a bonus.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Return. When does the train leave?

lines.speaker: Blagajničarka:
lines.text: Uro in pol. Z avtobusom je dlje.
lines.id: An hour and a half. It takes longer by bus.
lines.literal: hour-acc and half. with bus-ins is longer.

lines.speaker: Blagajničarka:
lines.id: It depends on the sound that comes after it.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Here you go. Thank you very much!

notes: **Z and s are the same word.** What decides which sound you use is the **first letter of the next word**, not the meaning. The rule is purely about ease of pronunciation: *s* before voiceless sounds, *z* before everything else. Slovenian does something similar with *iz/z*, *v/u* and *k/h*.

**Means of transport take the instrumental.** *Z vlakom*, *z avtobusom*, *s kolesom*, *z avtom*. Literally "with the train" — Slovenian treats a vehicle as a tool, just like a knife or a pen. One exception uses no preposition at all: *peš* (on foot).

**Koliko časa traja? uses the genitive.** You've known this since unit 5: *koliko* always pulls in that form. The answer, though, uses the accusative, because a length of time is treated as an object: *Traja uro in pol* (it takes an hour and a half), *Traja dve uri*.

**Uro in pol = an hour and a half.** Slovenian says "hour and half", just as English does. Other phrases on the same pattern: *dan in pol* (a day and a half), *leto in pol* (a year and a half). For just half: *pol ure*.

**Srečno pot!** — "have a lucky journey" — is what you'll hear every time you say goodbye at a station or airport. Its relatives: *Lep dan!*, *Lep večer!*, *Srečno!* All short, warm, and needing no answer other than *Hvala, enako!* (thanks, same to you).

grammars.title: Orodnik — the case of tools and company
body: The last case you need at A1. It marks **with what** or **with whom** something is done, and it also appears after position prepositions such as *pred*, *za*, *nad*, *pod* and *med*.

head: Type
Basic form
Instrumental
Example
rows: *Potujem z vlakom.* — I'm going by train.
*Grem z avtom.* — I'm going by car.
*Grem s prijateljem.* — I'm going with a friend.
*Plačam s kartico.* — I'll pay by card.
*Grem z Majo.* — I'm going with Maja.
*Pred pošto.* — In front of the post office.

after: There are only two endings: **-om** for masculine and neuter words (becoming **-em** after *c, č, j, š, ž*), and **-o** for feminine words. The last one happens to sound the same as the accusative — the preposition tells them apart: *Vidim Majo* (object) versus *Grem z Majo* (company).

With the instrumental, all six Slovenian cases have now passed before your eyes: **imenovalnik** (nominative: the subject), **rodilnik** (genitive: of, possession, negation), **dajalnik** (dative: to), **tožilnik** (accusative: object, direction), **mestnik** (locative: place), **orodnik** (instrumental: tool, company). The full summary is at the back of this course.

grammars.title: Z or s — the sound rule
body: This rule has nothing to do with meaning; it's purely about sound. Once you've seen the list, it stops feeling random.

head: Use
Before the sounds
Example
rows: p, t, k, s, š, c, č, f, h
b, d, g, z, ž, j, l, m, n, r, v

after: The cheapest way to remember it: **whispered sounds want *s*, voiced sounds want *z***. Put your hand on your throat — if it vibrates when you say the first letter, use *z*.
A similar rule applies to the pair **k / h** (to someone's place): *h* is used only before *k* and *g* — *h koncu*, *h gospe* — and *k* everywhere else: *k Maji*, *k zdravniku*.

blocks.text: Slovenia is roughly the size of New Jersey, so almost every destination is within two hours. The trains are run by **Slovenske železnice**; intercity buses are often faster than the train on the same route.

head: Sentence
Say it
Meaning
rows: Where do I have to change?
I'm going to miss the train!

blocks.text: The destinations people mention most: **Bled** and **Bohinj** in the mountains, **Piran** and **Portorož** on the coast, **Postojna** and **Škocjan** for caves, **Maribor** and **Ptuj** in the east, and **Trst** — the Slovenian name for Trieste in Italy, two hours from Ljubljana by bus.

blocks.text: Notice **zastonj** (free) — an everyday word heard far more often than the official *brezplačno*. And **prtljaga** (luggage) is one of the hardest words to pronounce in this whole course: **PUHRT-lyah-gah**, with a short "uh" before the *r*.

blocks.title: Good to know before you set off
items: Train tickets can be bought in the app or at the counter; if you board without one, buy it from the conductor **before** they come to you, or the fine applies.
Intercity buses leave from the **avtobusna postaja**, which in Ljubljana is right next to the train station. For Ljubljana city buses you need an **Urbana** card; cash isn't accepted on board.
To drive on the motorway you must have a **vinjeta** — a sticker or e-vignette. Without one the fine is steep, and checks are automatic.
